chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from one of our companions, who said:

Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) hosted a banquet for one of his sons, so he fed the people of the city faludhaj (a type of sweet dish) for three days in large bowls, in the mosques and the alleyways. Some of the people of the city criticized him for this.

So that reached him (peace be upon him), and he said: 'Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not grant anything to any of His prophets except that He granted Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) the like of it, and added to it what He did not grant them.'

He said to Sulayman (peace be upon him): 'This is Our gift, so bestow it or withhold it without measure.' And He said to Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family): 'And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and from whatever he forbids you, refrain.'

key_terms.أَوْلَمَ: Hosted a banquet or wedding feast

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam Musa al-Kazim justify his lavish banquet to the critics in Medina?
ai.summary: Imam Musa al-Kazim (peace be upon him) hosted a generous banquet for his son, feeding the people of Medina faludhaj for three days in public spaces like mosques and alleys. When some criticized this lavishness, he explained that God granted Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) all that He granted previous prophets and added more, citing Quranic verses about Sulayman's freedom of choice and Muhammad's absolute authority in receiving divine gifts. This narration highlights the Shia concept of 'Fadl' (superiority/excess) of the Prophet over previous prophets, linking the Imam's public generosity to the prophetic model of unrestricted divine bestowal.
